title: Federation & AI-trust readiness scorecard
intro: Ten questions across identity, trust, and supply chain. Runs entirely in your browser; on completion you may optionally share your anonymous answers (no identity, no free text) so we learn whether our guidance is on the mark.

questions.text: Do you operate a standards-based identity provider (OIDC or SAML)?

options.label: Yes — consolidated on one OIDC IdP
Several IdPs / mid-migration
options.guidance: Consolidating on one OIDC issuer first makes waypoint's audience/issuer checks simpler.

options.label: No standards-based IdP yet
options.guidance: Start with a managed OIDC provider (Entra, Google, Okta) — waypoint delegates login to it rather than reinventing it.

questions.text: Do the tokens your services accept enforce an audience (are they scoped to a specific resource)?

options.label: Tokens carry an audience but it isn't checked everywhere
options.guidance: An unchecked audience lets a token minted for one service be replayed at another — enforce it at every resource.

options.label: No audience scoping
options.guidance: Audience-restricted tokens (RFC 8707) are the baseline for safely exposing an MCP gateway.

questions.text: How do you decide which external tools / MCP servers to trust today?

options.label: Cryptographic verification against an anchor we control
A maintained allowlist of URLs
options.guidance: An allowlist is a good start; a trust chain makes the decision verifiable and revocable rather than manual.

options.label: Ad hoc — whoever provides the URL
options.guidance: This is precisely the assumption OpenID Federation replaces with verification.

questions.text: Would you want to run (or already run) your own trust anchor?

options.label: Yes — we require our own corporate anchor
Prefer a hosted anchor we don't operate
options.guidance: A hosted anchor is fine — the key is that you can still add your own to the accepted list (bring your own trust).

options.label: Not sure what that involves
options.guidance: Start local: fedmgr init mints a self-contained anchor on one machine so you can see the model before committing.

questions.text: If a trusted tool were compromised, how fast could you withdraw trust everywhere?

options.label: Revoke centrally; verifiers stop admitting it on next check
Manually update allowlists / redeploy
options.guidance: Manual withdrawal is slow and error-prone; anchor-side revocation consulted at verify time is near-instant.

options.label: We couldn't reliably
options.guidance: Revocation that verifiers actually consult on every check is a core reason to adopt a federation.

questions.text: Do your build artifacts ship with a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)?

options.label: SBOMs, but unsigned
options.guidance: An unsigned SBOM can be swapped; sign it (e.g. cosign) so it's bound to a signer.

options.label: No SBOMs
options.guidance: Start by generating one in CI with syft — it's the raw material for every later trust claim.

questions.text: Is there a vulnerability-scan gate that can block a release?

options.label: Yes — HIGH/CRITICAL findings block the release
We scan, but it's advisory
options.guidance: An advisory scan is a log, not a gate — make a failing scan actually stop issuance.

options.label: No scanning in the pipeline
options.guidance: A scan gate (e.g. trivy) enforcing zero HIGH/CRITICAL is the letsfederate SLA baseline.

questions.text: Can a consumer cryptographically bind an attestation to the exact artifact digest they run?

options.label: Yes — attestations reference the artifact digest
We produce attestations but they sit side by side
options.guidance: Bind them: one signed in-toto Statement over the artifact digest ties SBOM + scan + mark into a verifiable chain.

options.label: No attestations
options.guidance: Digest-bound attestation is what makes a trust mark mean 'this exact image passed', not 'something did'.

questions.text: Are AI assistants in your org already calling external MCP tool servers?

options.label: Yes — assistants connect directly
options.guidance: Direct connections skip verification entirely; a gateway (waypoint) is where admission and trust checks belong.

options.label: Not yet, but planning to
options.guidance: Put the gateway + trust model in place before the first server goes live — it's much harder to retrofit.

questions.text: Do you have a post-quantum crypto migration plan?

options.label: Aware of it, no plan yet
options.guidance: Start with a Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM) so you know which algorithms are quantum-vulnerable and by when.

options.label: Not on our radar
options.guidance: The 2026 federal timeline (key-establishment by 2030, signatures by 2031) makes a CBOM and crypto-agility worth starting now.

tiers.label: Federation-ready
tiers.blurb: You have the identity, trust, and supply-chain foundations. fedmgr is mostly about wiring what you already have into a verifiable chain — start with the trust-chain and digest-bound trust marks.

tiers.label: Emerging
tiers.blurb: Strong in places, gaps in others. Pick the lowest-scoring section and close it first — usually revocation or supply-chain binding — then stand up a local anchor to see the whole loop.

tiers.label: Building foundations
tiers.blurb: The pieces are worth assembling deliberately. Begin with a standards-based IdP and SBOMs in CI; those unlock everything downstream. Run fedmgr init locally to see the target state.

tiers.label: Explorer
tiers.blurb: Great time to learn the model before committing. Run the local lab, walk one trust chain end to end, and read the bring-your-own-trust arc — no infrastructure required.
